newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE - Morocco's ONA sheds fat to grow.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Morocco's ONA sheds fat to grow.

text.p: One of Africa's largest private conglomerates, Morocco's ONA Group, is spinning off loss-making subsidiaries to focus on its four core businesses.

ONA now owns stakes in more than 80 firms, with a consolidated turnover of 18.1 billion dirhams ($1.9 billion) in 1996. But it is shedding those which are not geared for maximum profits and which do not fit strategic plans to develop its business in international trading, mining, finance and agro-industry.

"ONA's policy aims at ceding non-strategic subsidiaries or firms showing structural losses, downsizing its debt, reducing costs and preserving and improving market share by taking into account consumers' interests," ONA's chairman Fouad Filali said.

Last year, the group disposed of stakes in Morocco's private 2M television station, and in local subsidiaries of a German car maker and French telecommunications company Alcatel. It also sold off its majority shares in the Somadim sugar company, OMACI canned fish company and printing firm Salimagraph.

Anas Alami, head of research at the Casablanca-based Upline Securities told Reuters: "A slight increase in turnover and improved margins should contribute to a 22 percent rise in earnings in 1997...We expect the conglomerate to reach 1.07 billion dirhams as net profit this year,"
In 1996 consolidated net profit rose 45.8 percent to 878.7 million dirhams.
FOCUS ON CORE BUSINESS
ONA launched a two-year strategic plan in 1995 to focus activity in four core sectors -- international business, mining, finance and agro-industry.
"The plan continues to target invested capital's profitability and setting up conditions for appreciation of share prices on the Casablanca bourse," the group said in a recent report.
The conglomerate has market capitalisation of around 14 billion dirhams, with 17.2 million issued shares. Last year some 3.0 million of its shares changed hands on the Casablanca exchange.
It has four subsidiaries listed on the stock exchange, of which three control domestic agro-industry.
ONA subsidiaries Cosumar sugar refinery and edible oil company Lesieur Cristal showed exceptional results in 1996, with net profit gains of 18.9 percent and 31.5 percent respectively.
"To preserve their profitability, Cosumar and Lesieur have resolutely been engaged in improving their productivity," an ONA senior manager said.

The other two listed subsidiaries, Centrale Laitiere milk company and Financiere Diwan, are expected to consolidate their domestic market shares in 1997 after good results last year, a stockbroker said.
LOCOMOTIVE OF MOROCCO'S ECONOMY

With its 1998-2000 strategic plan to be announced soon, ONA expects to dramatically cut its debt, expand its activity and focus on high-margin businesses to meet the challenges stemming from Morocco's opening to a globalised market.

It had debt of 1.7 billion dirhams in 1996 of which 1.5 billion dirhams is covered by arrears not yet paid by the state-owned compensation fund to ONA, an analyst at Casablanca Finance Intermediation said.
With positive prospects for world metal consumption and prices, the conglomerate expects its mining business to be the driving force behind increased business and profits this year.
Its consolidated mining turnover rose 5.8 percent to 1.05 billion dirhams in 1996.

ONA invests an average 100 million dirhams per year to improve the quality of its products in order to maintain a leading position in Morocco. It also targets African and European markets through its international unit, which comprises French-based Optorg, Peches et Froid and Fruit Expansion.
Filali, a son-in-law of King Hassan II, is considered the mastermind of the group's aggressive expansion policy since he took over the group's management in the late 1980s.
"ONA is the locomotive of Morocco's modern economy...We wish other national groups to follow our example to haul the kingdom's economy into the 21st century," Filali has said.
A majority stake of 54 percent of ONA's capital is controlled by Moroccan private institutions, including the royal family, which owns 13.7 percent.
($1 = 9.4 dirhams)
